cue: What do you say right before trying something that might not work?

es.text: Que sea lo que Dios quiera
es.literal: may it be what God wants
es.meaning: Said before a risky attempt: whatever happens, happens — spoken as a handing-over of the outcome.
es.example: Ya mandé la solicitud. Que sea lo que Dios quiera.
es.exampleTranslation: I've sent the application off. Here goes nothing.

it.text: Che Dio ce la mandi buona
it.literal: may God send it to us good
it.meaning: Said before a risky attempt: let's hope this goes well.
it.example: Ho mandato la domanda. Che Dio ce la mandi buona.
it.exampleTranslation: I've sent the application off. Here goes nothing.

sources.headword: che Dio ce la mandi buona

bridge.note: Both languages hand the outcome to God at the same moment — the breath before you press send — and they hand it over in opposite postures. Spanish surrenders: let it be whatever God wants, the speaker stepping back and accepting in advance. Italian asks: may God send it to us good, a petition with a preference attached. One resigns, the other lobbies. Same faith, same nerves, and a different relationship with the management.

interference.es_to_it: The Italian has a pronoun cluster with nothing behind it: ce LA mandi buona, where la is feminine and refers to no noun at all — the situation, roughly, left unnamed. Spanish has no equivalent and no way to derive it, so the phrase has to be learned whole. Note also that Italian names a preference (buona) where Spanish does not.
interference.it_to_es: Spanish stacks two subjunctives in a row — que SEA lo que Dios QUIERA — and accepts any outcome rather than requesting a good one. Reaching for the Italian shape and saying 'que Dios nos la mande buena' will be understood as an odd calque. Spanish has other ways of handing an outcome over, some of them inherited from Arabic rather than Latin, and they do not all invoke God.

review.notes: Drafted by Claude 2026-08-01 from an English seed ('here goes nothing'), so BOTH sides were found rather than one being given — a different provenance from the reviewer batches and worth noting. IT SIDE HAS DIRECT ATTESTATION OF THE EQUIVALENCE: Reverso's parallel corpus shows Italian subtitles rendering 'HERE GOES NOTHING' as 'Che Dio ce la mandi buona'. That is a translation corpus, not a dictionary, so the citation is tier-Corpus; a Treccani entry under `Dio` or `mandare` would be better if one exists — PLEASE CHECK. ES side is the consensus of a WordReference thread of native speakers, several of whom independently offered 'que sea lo que Dios quiera' as the closest fit, one citing the published Spanish translation of Dan Brown's Inferno. Also weak sourcing; RAE may carry nothing under `Dios` for this. BOTH SIDES NEED PROPER CITATIONS BEFORE APPROVAL. REGISTER QUESTION FOR BOTH REVIEWERS: these are religious invocations used by secular speakers, which is normal in both languages, but confirm neither reads as devout rather than idiomatic — a subscriber saying this to an actually religious colleague should not land oddly. ALTERNATIVES CONSIDERED: secular options exist on both sides ('a ver qué pasa', 'allá voy' / 'vada come vada', 'speriamo bene') and would make a blander, safer pair with no bridge in it. If the reviewers judge the religious framing too strong, that is the fallback. NOT PAIRED WITH 'sea lo que sea', which would collide with 0253 and 0256, both drafted today.
